Romualdo Ricardo Jiménez Oreamuno was a Costa Rican lawyer and statesman who served as President of Costa Rica on three separate occasions: 1910–1914, 1924–1928, and 1932–1936. He was a key figure in Costa Rican liberal politics, affiliated with the Republican Party and later the National Republican Party. Jiménez was elected to the Constitutional Congress on three occasions and held key positions in the executive and judicial branches.

Born on February 6, 1859, in Cartago, Costa Rica, Jiménez Oreamuno studied law at the University of Costa Rica and later became a prominent lawyer in the country. He entered politics in the late 1800s and quickly rose through the ranks, serving as a member of the Legislative Assembly and later as the Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Jiménez Oreamuno's presidency was marked by significant economic growth, infrastructure development, and social reform. He implemented various policies aimed at reducing poverty and inequality, including the creation of a social security system and the expansion of education and healthcare.

Despite his achievements, Jiménez Oreamuno faced significant challenges during his presidency, including a major earthquake in 1914 and the Great Depression in the 1930s. He also had to navigate complex relationships with neighboring countries, including Nicaragua and the United States.

After leaving office, Jiménez Oreamuno continued to be active in politics, serving as a member of the Constitutional Congress and later as the Minister of Justice. He died on January 4, 1945, at the age of 85.

Jiménez Oreamuno's legacy as a statesman and lawyer has endured in Costa Rica, and he remains one of the country's most respected and influential figures. His commitment to social justice and economic development continues to inspire politicians and citizens alike.
